title: Method to systematically investigate the effect of tramp elements in resistance spot welding
abstract:
Abstract
 With the increasing utilisation of scrap in metallurgical processes due to recycling to reduce CO 2  footprint, the content of tramp elements in the base material is increasing. In order to quickly investigate the influence of tramp elements on the weld nugget microstructure and mechanical properties during resistance spot welding (RSW), a method has been developed to introduce tramp elements into the weld nugget. By making an indentation in one of the two sheets to be welded and inserting the desired quantity of tramp element before welding, the weld nugget can specifically be alloyed. This allows to quickly analyse the influence of individual tramp elements on the microstructure and its influence on the resulting mechanical properties. The applicability of the method was investigated using Cu as tramp element material. As part of the investigations, a targeted Cu content of 0.4 wt% was set, which was confirmed using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The spot welds alloyed according to the method were compared with spot welds without the Cu addition and spot welds of an already Cu-alloyed material. The weld nugget microstructure of all steels analysed by light optical microscopy (LOM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was martensitic with similar grain size and morphology, regardless of the Cu content. In tensile shear (TS) and cross tension (CT), testing plug failure occurred in all samples. The results from the TS tests with peak forces of 11.4–12.2 kN and absorption energies between 14.3 and 18.5 J were very close to each other. The CT results with peak forces of 6.7–8.5 kN and energies between 46 and 69 J showed a similar picture. The average weld nugget hardness of all three weld configurations was in between 383 and 398 HV1. The microstructural and mechanical results showed no significant differences. The presented method for a targeted weld nugget alloying during resistance spot welding allows a repeatable, easy and quick investigation of the influence of alloy modification by tramp elements such as Cu on the weld nugget properties and offers a practical approach to assess material changes due to an increased tramp element content.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Due to the ongoing need for reducing the greenhouse gas emissions, the steel industry is in change and many European steel plants are going through a technology switch from the basic oxygen furnace (BOF) to steel production with an electric arc furnace (EAF) based on scrap as raw material. Experience has shown that with the higher amount of scrap used in steel production, the amount of tramp elements in the finished steel product has risen. Some of them can be removed during the follow-up processes but elements like copper (Cu), molybdenum (Mo), nickel (Ni) or tin (Sn) are non-removable or only removable to a limited extent. To guarantee a proper steel performance, it is crucial to understand the effect of those tramp elements on mechanical properties and the further processability, like forming processes or weldability [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ].

In the automotive industry, resistance spot welding (RSW) is the main joining method used to join a broad variety of steel grades, mainly advanced high strength steels (AHSS) [ 4 ]. Some previous studies are dealing with the effect of tramp elements on the weldability of steel but mostly during arc welding and not RSW. In RSW, the amount of alloying and tramp elements can influence the welding lobe curve [ 5 ,  6 ], the liquid metal embrittlement behavior [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ], the weld nugget strength and the failure behavior [ 10 ,  11 ] which are all weldability indicators.

In this study, the main object is to utilise a method to quickly and reliably investigate the influence of tramp elements during RSW. To evaluate the influence of tramp elements, usually small cast ingots with the desired element contents are cast and then further processed on small-scale aggregates to imitate a large-scale steel production. The production of small-scale casts is a time-consuming process and can last up to several months. To avoid significant delay in the development process, a new method is introduced by using an interlayer in a reservoir during the RSW process. A brief list of literature elaborating the methods of interlayers in RSW is shown in Table  1 .

As introduced above, alloying of the weld nugget in previous research topics is mainly realised by using interlayers of different thickness between the sheets to be welded. Usually, they are used in dissimilar metal welds to avoid the formation of intermetallic phases and enable welding. They are also used for martensitic stainless steels to enhance the weldability and the fracture behavior of spot welds by introducing Ni into the weld nugget to change the weld nugget microstructure. The main interlayer material used is Ni, in different thicknesses to change the weld nugget microstructure from martensite to austenite and enhance the failure behavior. In the work of Aghajani [ 14 ,  15 – 16 ], the Ni interlayer thickness is varied from 50 to 400 µm to rise the Ni content in the weld nugget and therefore change the failure behavior from an interfacial failure to a plug failure. The measured Ni content in the weld nugget varied from 4.9 to 27.7 wt%. With rising Ni content, rising tensile shear strength (TSS) and energy absorption as well as rising cross tension strength (CTS) and energy absorption compared to the material without interlayer were observed.

Although this approach is already known to introduce different elements in the weld nugget, it is impractical to achieve very low amounts of alloying elements in the range tramp elements usually occur in steel. To vary the tramp element content and to alloy very small amounts, very thin interlayers, which are unpractical to handle, would be necessary. Additionally, elements with low melting temperatures are prone to a displacement out of the faying surface. To achieve a targeted introduction of the element into the weld nugget and avoid losses due to displacement, a new approach is presented in this work.

The new method was tested with the element Cu and how it affects the weld nugget during RSW. In general, Cu is austenite stabilising, weakens the grain boundary cohesion, amplifies the corrosion resistance and amplifies the strength through solid solution strengthening and precipitation hardening if enough Cu is available, and the right heat treatment is applied [ 22 ]. It is known for its negative influence on hot workability caused by hot shortness, this effect can already occur from 0.2 wt% Cu [ 23 ,  24 ]. Cu-associated effects during welding mainly occur from precipitation due to long welding times and post weld heat treatments, which is not relevant for RSW due to the short process times. Even small amounts of Cu (from 0.5 wt%) can cause precipitation hardening in the heat-affected zone (HAZ) as well as grain refinement of the weld microstructure. Precipitation hardening usually occurs after a post weld heat treatment or in multiple-layer welds. Due to the precipitation hardening, the HAZ strength increases while the toughness decreases [ 25 ,  26 – 27 ]. Copper also slightly increases the hot cracking tendency, the hardness through solid solution hardening, and improves grain refinement across all welding zones [ 27 ,  28 ]. According to Becker [ 28 ], the addition of up to 0.85 wt% Cu does not seem to have any negative effects on the weld metal and HAZ during welding.

sections.heading: Materials and experimental procedure
paragraphs: Materials used for the experiments are listed in Table  2 . Both are dual-phase steels from a standard galvanising production line and have a thickness of 1 mm with a zinc coating thickness of 50 g/m 2 . Steel A and steel B were both produced at industrial scale via the conventional blast furnace-basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF) route. The only difference between them is that steel B was deliberately alloyed with copper (Cu) in order to investigate its influence on the material’s properties.

Table 2  Chemical composition and mechanical properties of metal sheets and insert material Material Chemical composition [wt.%] Mechanical properties Fe C Mn+Cr Si Cu YS [MPa] UTS [MPa] TEL [%] Steel A Balance 0,080 2,21 0,23 0,01 368 633 26,5 Steel B Balance 0,087 2,01 0,2 0,35 369 625 27,2 Cu-foil - - - - 99,9 n.a. n.a. n.a.

Steel A was used as reference material and for the Cu alloying experiments. The Cu material used to alloy the weld nugget was a 99.9 wt% Cu foil with a thickness of 0.01 mm. Steel B is equivalent to steel A in terms of steel grade, yet it possesses a higher Cu content of 0.35 wt%. It exhibits a compensated chemical composition, which serves to counteract the hardening effect of Cu. This steel is utilised for the purpose of comparison with steel A and steel A + Cu foil alloyed weld nuggets. Therefore, three different weld configurations are compared to each other, steel A welds, steel B welds and steel A + Cu foil welds.

Resistance spot welding was performed using a NIMAK PMP 6–2/250MF pedestal mid-frequency 1000-Hz spot welding machine with a Matuschek SilverSPATZ M600LL controller. At first, the weld current range of both steels (A and B) were determined according to the SEP 1220–2:2011 [ 29 ] procedure with an F1-16–20-6 electrode which is tip dressed to 5.5 mm. The electrode force of 3.5 kN, a squeezing time of 600 ms, a welding time of 260 ms and a holding time of 120 ms was used, therefore. For both materials, a weld current range from 6.2 to 8.1 kA was determined. All further welding experiments were carried out using the same welding times and electrode force at a welding current of 8 kA. This high current is used to obtain a large weld nugget but still avoid expulsion. Samples with and without Cu addition were welded with the same welding parameters.

The Cu addition was realised by circular foil cut-outs of different sizes by hand-held punch hole pliers (Fig.  3  a–b). The size and number of Cu foil cutouts are selected depending on how much Cu is to be alloyed in the weld nugget. The average mass of 3-mm and 2-mm cut-outs was determined using five cut-outs per diameter, weighing them on a precision balance. The average weight is shown in Table  3 . Fig. 3 a  Circular Cu-cutouts in 3 and 2 mm,  b  handheld punch-hole pliers. Table 3 Average Cu-cutout weight of different cutout diameters Cut-out diameter [mm] 3 2 Average cut-out weight [mg] 0.53 ± 0.01 0.20 ± 0.02

To compare the Cu-alloyed steel A weld nugget with the already Cu-containing welds of steel B, a Cu content of around 0.4 wt% was aimed for by putting two 3-mm cut-outs in the indentation. According to Eq. (2.1), the so calculated Cu content of the weld nugget would be 0.43 wt%.

Optical images of the TS and CT failures were carried out using a Keyence VHX-X1 microscope. Metallographic examinations for light optical microscopy (LOM) were carried out using a 3% HNO 3  etchant and an etching time of 5 s. Scanning electron microscopy examinations were carried out by a Zeiss ultra55 SEM. For the SEM examinations, the samples were electropolished with a Struers LectroPol-5 and the Struers A3 electrolyte. Chemical composition of the weld microstructure was determined using an Oxford X-Max 50 mm 2  energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) detector at a working distance of 9.6 mm and an acceleration voltage of 20 kV.

The mechanical properties of the spot-welded samples were examined using Vickers microhardness measurements and tensile shear (TS) and cross tension (CT) tests. Microhardness testing was carried out by Vickers microhardness measurement across the weld nugget by a load of 9.81 N for 10 s. CT and TS specimen dimensions are schematically shown in Fig.  4  and testing speed was 10 mm/min. The peak load and the failure energies were measured, as well as the failure behavior was observed to evaluate the mechanical properties. Fig. 4 Cross tension (CT) and shear tensile (TS) test specimen dimensions

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs: In Fig.  2 a and b, the weld nugget dimensions of the weld nuggets seen in Fig.  6 a, e and j utilised by the software ImageJ are shown. The diameter and thickness of the weld nuggets for the three spot welded configurations are found to be highly comparable. The introduction of a copper foil during RSW does not result in any alteration of the dimensions. The diameter of all weld nuggets is approximately 5.8 mm, and the thickness is approximately 1.2 mm.

sections.heading: EDS measurements
paragraphs: The chemical composition of the weld nuggets was determined via scans of three different areas in the weld nugget according to Fig.  5 . Figure  5 (1–3) shows the measured EDS spectra of the three measuring positions of the Cu foil added sample and Table  4  shows the Cu content of the different spot welds (steel A, steel B, steel A + Cu foil) at the three measuring positions. In the Cu foil–alloyed sample, Cu content varies between 0.3 wt% and 0.5 wt% at an average of 0.4 wt% which fits well with the calculated 0.425 wt% of the estimated results. The Cu distribution across the various measuring points is also quite homogeneous and probably due to mixing caused by strong convection in the liquid weld nugget due to the magnetic field occurring through the passage of the current [ 30 ]. The measurements also correspond to the given chemical composition in Table  2 . In steel A, no Cu was found due to the low Cu amount and in steel B around 0.3 wt% to 0.4 wt% was detected. sections.heading: Microstructural analysis
paragraphs: Figure  6  shows the weld macro- and microstructure of steel A (a–d), steel B (e–h) and steel A + Cu foil (i–l) spot welds. The LOM images of all samples (Fig.  6 a, b, e, f, i, j) are showing a homogeneous martensite microstructures through the whole fusion zone (FZ). No residual Cu could be observed in the steel A + Cu foil samples which indicates that the entirety of the Cu was melted and alloyed with the weld nugget. The images of steel B (Fig.  6 e, f) appear darker in the LOM; this is attributed to an etching effect rather than a different microstructure. The SEM images (Fig.  6 c, d, g, h, k, l) show a full martensite microstructure with tempered martensite areas across all samples. The occurrence of tempered martensite is attributed to the phenomenon of auto-tempering. The initial martensite that is formed at martensite start temperature is tempered during the subsequent cooling process when the temperatures remain sufficiently elevated [ 31 ]. Fig. 6 Weld microstructures of steel A ( a – d ), steel B ( e – h ) and steel A + Cu foil ( i – l ). LOM images ( a ,  b ,  e ,  f ,  i ,  j ) and SEM images ( c ,  d ,  g ,  h ,  k ,  l ). ( α ′: martensite;  α ′ T : tempered martensite)

The images correspond to the expected microstructure of the materials, without significant differences in phase distribution or grain size. Compared to the steel A weld, the Cu-alloyed weld nuggets of steel B and steel A + Cu foil appear to have a less pronounced carbide structure in the tempered martensite. Overall, the microstructures of these three welds are very similar and no influence of Cu can be detected neither in the material already alloyed with Cu nor in the material alloyed with Cu foil.

This outcome is in accordance with the prevailing expectations. No significant deviations were observed in the microstructure. As indicated in the literature, only at higher Cu contents of around 1 wt% and above a significant effect is observed on the microstructure, due to the effect of lowering the transformation temperatures and grain refinement [ 32 ]. Influence of Cu precipitation only occurs from 0.6 wt% in combination with a suitable heat treatment [ 23 ,  25 ].

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs: The mechanical properties were obtained using Vickers microhardness measurements and TS and CT tests. The microhardness measurements are shown in Fig. 7 a and b. The average weld nugget (WN) hardness lies between 383 and 398 HV1, where steel A welds have a slightly harder fusion zone than steel B and steel A + Cu foil welds. However, the hardness measurements of the three configurations are very similar across the WN, heat-affected zone (HAZ) and the base metal (BM) and can be categorised within the typical measurement scatter. Fig. 7 a  Average weld nugget microhardness and  b  microhardness values of the RSW joints.

The load displacement curves of three parallel samples of each configuration are shown in Fig.  8 a and c and the average peak load and energy absorption during TS and CT tests are shown in Fig.  8 b and d. As can be seen in Fig.  8 a, the TSS load displacement curves of steel A, steel B and steel A + Cu foil are very similar. The maximum TSS were in the range of 11.4–11.9 kN and the average energy absorption at maximum force were between 16.1 and 17.4 J. The CT tests show a similar picture to the TS results (Fig. 8 c). Here the result is mainly influenced by the fact that the crosshead displacement is measured rather than the displacement of the specimen. It can be observed that the maximum force and the absorbed energy increase slightly from steel A to steel B to steel A + Cu foil, but all in all do not differ significantly from each other. The maximum force and failure energy at max. force is shown in Fig.  8 d and are between 7.6 and 8.2 kN and absorbed energy of 56–66 J. All samples failed in plug failure and are shown in Fig.  9 a–i for TS and Fig.  10 a–i for CT tests. The failure exhibited by the TS and CT tests did not show any significant differences, and their visual appearance seems quite similar. This finding underscores the comparable failure characteristics of the samples and confirms the previously determined similar mechanical properties.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs:
The results of the three different spot-welding configurations of steel A, steel B and steel A + Cu foil showed a comparable behavior over all tests (see Table  5 ). The weld nugget dimension as well as the microstructure and the mechanical properties like TSS, absorbed TS energy, CTS, absorbed CT energy, fracture behavior and Vickers microhardness do not differ significantly. The deviations observed are within the range of natural variation.
 Table 5 Overview of mechanical properties, WN size and Cu content of the tested configurations Weld configuration Cu content [wt%] WN diameter [mm] WN thickness [mm] TSS [kN] TS energy [J] CTS [kN] CT energy [J] WN hardness [HV1] failure mode Steel A 0.01 5.72 ± 0.15 1.19 ± 0.05 11.4 ± 0.04 16.1 ± 1.2 7.6 ± 0.6 56 ± 6.7 398.6 ± 19.4 PF Steel B 0.35 5.84 ± 0.04 1.16 ± 0.01 11.9 ± 0.20 17.4 ± 0.8 7.8 ± 0.5 58.9 ± 6.1 386.2 ± 14.5 PF Steel A  +  Cu foil 0.4 5.83 ± 0.14 1.17 ± 0.02 11.9 ± 0.01 17.2 ± 0.1 8.2 ± 0.3 66 ± 3.2 383.5 ± 9.1 PF

Although the presented method worked quite well, it is not possible to evaluate the influence of various tramp elements using this method alone. It is important to note that the weld nugget is the only component being alloyed, and it is not possible to check the influences of tramp elements on the heat-affected zone, which is mainly cited for the influence of Cu in literature. According to the CT and TS results due to the PF failure characteristic, in which the material fractures within the HAZ, the mechanical response of the HAZ is assessed rather than that of the alloyed weld nugget. Nevertheless, this behavior can serve as an additional indication for identifying critical tramp elements or their critical concentrations. A change of the failure mode from PF to a fracture mode that propagates through the weld nugget would imply that the tramp element, or its amount, significantly weakens the nugget region. This enables a screening approach to determine which tramp elements and concentrations are critical. The method provides a quick investigation on how tramp elements can behave and gives an initial result. In a second step, the influence on the heat-affected zone can then be analysed using small cast ingots.

In summary, a method of alloying Cu into the weld nugget during RSW of a CMnSi steel has been tested to investigate the influence of Cu on the weld nugget in terms of microstructure and mechanical properties. Using this method, 1-mm-thick metal sheets were welded and microstructural evaluation with LOM and SEM + EDS, as well as the mechanical performance, was investigated using CT and TS tests and Vickers microhardness measurements. The following conclusions are drawn: A Cu content of 0.4 wt% was selectively alloyed into the weld nugget of steel A by inserting Cu foil into a pre-grained reservoir. The previously calculated Cu content was confirmed by EDS analysis. This approach showed a high degree of repeatability. The addition of Cu showed no significant change in the weld nugget microstructure, which is in agreement with the behavior of the Cu-alloyed steel variant (B). The fusion zone microstructure of all spot welds is martensitic with tempered martensite fractions. Vickers microhardness measurements showed no significant difference between the three tested configurations. The mechanical performance during TS and CT tests showed marginal yet non-significant increase in peak load and energy absorption for the Cu-containing samples, including both the already Cu-alloyed steel B samples and those that have been alloyed using the method described in this study (steel A + Cu foil). A plug failure was observed for all samples.

The study concluded that the presence of Cu, whether inherent in the material or alloyed with foils, has no significant influence on the joint microstructure and mechanical behavior. The results obtained are readily comparable and suggest that the influence of Cu on the microstructure and mechanical properties during RSW can be demonstrated with the method presented here up to a Cu content of 0.4 wt%. To account for potential effects of the added Cu foil on the texture within the weld nugget and to obtain a more detailed understanding of the microstructural evolution, additional characterisation methods, such as EBSD analysis, will be employed in upcoming investigations. In the future, the method also offers the possibility to test higher Cu contents like 1 wt% and other tramp elements to further investigate weld nugget behavior and to determine property changing tramp element contents.
